title: Rome too admits none can stand without divine pardon
source_text: XXXIII. Atque hic quoque est tanta vis veritatis, & tam vividus conscientiae sensus, ut ultro ei dent manus, nec repugnare audeant, etiam qui plurimum justitiae inhaerenti tribuere videntur. Nam Doctores Scholae Romanae agnoscunt neminem, per justitiam sibi inhaerentem & infusam, posse in judicio divino subsistere, siquidem Deus severe & absque misericordia, agere cum homine velit. Probant enim illud Gregorii primi, Omnis humana justitia, si districtum Dei judicium requiratur, injustitia esse convincitur. Et ultro fatentur, ac docent hominem quemlibet egere divina condonatione, non tantum respectu peccatorum illorum quae justifica-tionem illius praecesserunt: sed etiam propter lapsus varios ex infirmitate, in quos, etiam postquam justificatus est, identidem incidit; & propter quos merito coelo excluderetur, nisi clementia divina subveniret.
pass_a_gloss: And here too the force of truth is so great, and the sense of conscience so vivid, that even those who seem to attribute most to inherent righteousness freely give it their hands and dare not resist. For the doctors of the Roman School acknowledge that no one, by the righteousness inherent and infused in him, can stand in the divine judgment if God should wish to deal with man severely and without mercy. For they prove that saying of Gregory the First: All human righteousness, if God's strict judgment be required, is convicted of being injustice. And they freely confess and teach that every man needs divine pardon, not only with respect to those sins which preceded his justification, but also because of various falls from weakness into which, even after he has been justified, he repeatedly falls; and for which he would deservedly be shut out of heaven unless divine clemency came to his aid.
pass_b_english: Even strong assertors of inherent justice concede none can stand if God judges without mercy.
Gregory: all human justice is injustice under strict judgment; post-justification falls still need pardon.

choices.why: Key lemma for De Justitia densify §1067.
